brief.head: Statement of purpose
brief.text: Springsteen wanted each record to be a state­ment of pur­pose, Amit Varma read, with­out being “damned by the term con­cept album”. {013-C03}

brief.head: Scarcity’s gift
brief.text: The old world’s scarcity cre­ated a few focal points of shared cul­ture, Ajay Shah said: *Independence Day* means some­thing to both hosts. {013-C13}

brief.head: Strangers’ eyes
brief.text: Growing up means mov­ing be­yond self-centredness, Ajay Shah said, riff­ing on a Roger Waters line. Springsteen’s songs of or­di­nary peo­ple showed him the beauty and magic in everyone’s lives. {013-C14}

brief.head: Copy it out by hand
brief.text: A stu­dent in Amit Varma’s writ­ing course, whose first lan­guage is Hindi, copied Agota Kristof’s sen­tences out by hand to get the book’s rhythm into her head. {013-S14}

brief.head: The shortest highway
brief.text: Springsteen wrote that the E Street or­gan­ist Danny Federici had “the short­est high­way be­tween his fin­gers and his heart”, Amit Varma re­called. {013-J19}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: I work to be an an­ces­tor.
thought.who: Bruce Springsteen, as read by Amit Varma: refusing to let his father’s ghosts have the last word

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on Bruce Springsteen’s songs
lead.head: Rock and roll, by the book

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 13

body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah timed this one to a birth­day. Varma said the episode would come out on 22 September, the eve of Bruce Springsteen’s birth­day, a date he has al­ways known: his mother shares it.
When Bob Dylan won the Nobel Prize for lit­er­a­ture, many peo­ple were shocked, Varma said. He wrote an im­pas­sioned de­fence.
“To me, lit­er­a­ture is words,” he said. “Literature is words, and below that, lit­er­a­ture is sto­ry­telling.” Shakespeare, after all, wrote plays to be per­formed and read aloud. {013-C01}

Shah had two thoughts the mo­ment Dylan won, he said: yes, that is lit­er­a­ture; and Dylan be­fore Springsteen? “It should have been the other way around.” That, he told lis­ten­ers, is how two un­likely char­ac­ters came to make this pod­cast.
## An eye-opener on a mini-CD
Shah’s ac­count was per­sonal. Seniors in his col­lege hos­tel bought the LP of *Born in the USA* in 1984, but at the time he had ears only for Pink Floyd.

As a grad­u­ate stu­dent in America, he and Susan found a mini-CD with a live, acous­tic *Born to Run*: “only Mr. Springsteen play­ing the mouth organ and a gui­tar and singing all by him­self”. {013-S01}

It was an eye-opener. A three-CD live set fol­lowed, though Led Zeppelin had his ears then and Springsteen stayed a sideshow. Years later, at the Ministry of Finance in Delhi, the old al­bums started “com­ing to life” for him one by one.
## Four parts of a writer
Varma said he had no such co­her­ent nar­ra­tive. He of­fered four as­pects of Springsteen’s work in­stead: the ef­fort he made, the songs he wrote, the lan­guage he used and the change he em­braced.

The ef­fort came from the mem­oir, *Born to Run*: a rented gui­tar, an out­played band, a song writ­ten in ten min­utes. “Another way of think­ing about it,” Varma said, “is that it took 30 years to write the song.” {013-C05}

The songs came from the peo­ple around him: his sister’s teenage mar­riage, his father’s para­noia, his blue-collar town. When writ­ing stu­dents ask Varma what to write about, he tells them to look around them.
The lan­guage was plain. Springsteen never uses a word his lis­ten­ers can­not un­der­stand, Varma said, yet he goes “a level deeper than you ex­pect”. {013-C08}
He would never use a word like “poly­glot”, Varma added, as Shah had at the start of the show. Springsteen knows what it means. He has just never used it.
And the change was con­stant. Springsteen re­fused to play “cover ver­sions of him­self”, and there are dozens of ver­sions of *The River*.
## Ghosts and an­ces­tors
The hosts ended where the mem­oir does some of its hard­est work: with a fa­ther.

Springsteen wrote that in anal­y­sis “you work to turn the ghosts that haunt you into an­ces­tors who ac­com­pany you”. Then: “I work to be an an­ces­tor.” Varma saw a man aware of him­self as a char­ac­ter in a longer story. {013-C12}

Shah turned one of their own lines around. Each of us is a lin­ear com­bi­na­tion of our in­flu­ences; each of us is also adding to ev­ery­one else’s. So, he said, we should be the best ver­sion of our­selves.

Both closed on fa­thers and sons. Shah rec­om­mended *Independence Day*, Cat Stevens’s *Father and Son* and Cormac McCarthy’s *The Road*. Varma read A.K. Ramanujan’s *Self-Portrait*, about a face in a shop win­dow “often signed in a cor­ner by my fa­ther”.

second.label: The critic’s night
second.head: The future was on first
second.deck: Amit Varma on Jon Landau’s legendary review, and a partnership born of chance

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Jon Landau’s legendary review

body: On 9 May 1974, Bruce Springsteen and the E Street Band opened for Bonnie Raitt. A young critic, Jon Landau, wrote a re­view that Amit Varma read out, in­clud­ing: “I saw rock and roll’s fu­ture, and his name is Bruce Springsteen.” {#future}

Landau was 27; Springsteen was 25. {#landauage} Springsteen, who never re­ally had a fa­ther, saw him as one, and wrote that Landau was the first per­son he met “who had a lan­guage for dis­cussing these ideas and the life of the mind”.

Ajay Shah was re­minded of G. H. Hardy and Ramanujan: fas­ci­na­tion with a ge­nius, and care not to dis­rupt it. “I’m just so struck by this hap­pen­stance sort of con­nec­tion,” Varma said. {013-S02}

quote.text: Both the pas­sion of the fan and at the same time that abil­ity to step back and note the craft

third.head: Cover star, empty pockets

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Springsteen’s years of back taxes

body: In 1975 Bruce Springsteen was on the cov­ers of *Time* and *Newsweek*. Then the tax au­thor­i­ties came knock­ing for back taxes. *Born to Run*, *Darkness on the Edge of Town* and *The River* were all huge suc­cesses, Amit Varma said, but until 1982 Springsteen did not make a sin­gle paisa. {#broke}

The lean years went back a long way. His early band, Steel Mill, found a club where no­body went and of­fered to play there, charg­ing a dol­lar a head. Fifteen peo­ple came. The five mem­bers took $3 each. {#dollar}
Had *Born in the USA* flopped, Varma said, Springsteen would have been broke. “And that’s just a crazy thought.” {013-S13}
Ajay Shah drew a les­son for India, where ev­ery­body crit­i­cises the in­come tax au­thor­i­ties: “tax­men ev­ery­where can be pretty cruel”.

p2.deck: How Ajay Shah found Springsteen, and Amit Varma’s case in four parts: effort, songs, language and change

from1.head: Rock and roll, by the book

quote.text: I learned in that pe­riod that a record pro­ducer is ac­tu­ally like a co-author.

box.title: Springsteen in his own words
box.text: Amit Varma read from Bruce Springsteen’s au­to­bi­og­ra­phy, *Born to Run*, all through the episode. Of its pas­sage on writ­ing the title song, he said: “ev­ery­one should buy that book and read it to un­der­stand artis­tic process.” {#process}

sections.label: The listener
sections.head: Unplugged, then switched on
sections.caption: how he came to Springsteen
body: Ajay Shah came to Bruce Springsteen slowly, and the songs switched on in his mind one by one, years apart.

As a grad­u­ate stu­dent in America, he found a mini-CD of a 1988 show at the Los Angeles Coliseum, right next to his uni­ver­sity. He had not gone. On it was an acous­tic *Born to Run* that re­cast a song he had not liked on the album. {013-S01}
## A pro­ducer is an au­thor

Shah drew on his own trade. If some­one did for his re­search pa­pers what a pro­ducer does for a band, he said, they would get au­thor­ship. George Martin for the Beatles and Brian Eno for U2 were “first-class par­tic­i­pants in the cre­ative jour­ney”. {013-C02}

His own habit is to col­lect every live per­for­mance of one song and hear them in order. “No man can sing the same song twice,” he said. *Jungleland* in 1976 is bril­liant; in 2012 a grown man tells a dif­fer­ent story. {013-S11}

Long songs are a genre by them­selves, Shah ar­gued. *Stairway to Heaven* starts with an alaap and builds; *Jungleland* runs in re­verse, from a wall of sound through what Springsteen calls the world’s great­est sax­o­phone solo to the alaap at the end. {013-C04}

~ In Udaipur for a con­fer­ence, lines from its close sur­faced in his head: the poets around here “don’t write noth­ing at all. They just stand by and let it all be.” Between ses­sions, he played the song over and over.

quote.text: I learned in that pe­riod that a record pro­ducer is ac­tu­ally like a co-author.

sections.label: Aspect one: effort
sections.head: No natural genius, all graft
sections.caption: the work behind the genius
body: Rock stars seem to make it at 23, Amit Varma said; we don’t see that they have been at it since seven. The Beatles played hun­dreds and thou­sands of shows in Hamburg. Mozart was com­pos­ing at five.

Springsteen, by his own ac­count, was no nat­u­ral ge­nius. When Steel Mill was out­played at a San Francisco au­di­tion, bet­ter tal­ent did not scare him; what both­ered him was “not max­i­miz­ing my own abil­i­ties”. He went home know­ing there would have to be changes. {013-S04}

Not ev­ery­thing was laboured. He wrote *Hungry Heart* in about ten min­utes, and Bob Clearmountain mixed it in thirty sec­onds. Yet Springsteen wrote that they “could never have worked with Bob”, who was too fast; the E Street way was the hard way. {013-S07}
## A hun­dred Taj Mahals

Ajay Shah added a prin­ci­ple from chess and poker: vol­ume. {#volume} Build not one Taj Mahal but a hun­dred, he said, be­cause the oth­ers will fall by the way­side, and re­fine­ment comes from it­er­a­tion.

Craft also com­pounds. In S. Chandrasekhar’s *Truth and Beauty*, Shah found Beethoven telling a friend, be­fore the Ninth Symphony, that he now knew how to write music. He felt the same on first hear­ing *Devils and Dust*. {013-S12}
~ Varma’s moral for would-be artists was blunt: “boss, it takes work, it takes in­ten­tion­al­ity.”

quote.text: I had only one tal­ent. I was not a nat­u­ral ge­nius. I would have to use every ounce of what was in me.
quote.who: Bruce Springsteen, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: Aspect two: songs
sections.head: All in the family
sections.caption: a sister, a father and a town
body: Springsteen did not reach for myths or grand nar­ra­tives, Amit Varma said. He turned to the peo­ple around him: his sis­ter, his mother, his fa­ther and his small-town friends.

His fa­ther slid into para­noia, at one point be­liev­ing love songs on the radio were a gov­ern­ment ploy to get peo­ple mar­ried so they would pay more taxes. “I’m pre­sum­ing there are greater taxes in­volved there,” Varma said. {013-J08}

In the mem­oir, a friendly box­ing les­son in the liv­ing room turns when his father’s open-palm punches land a lit­tle too hard. The boy sees he is “an in­truder, a stranger, a com­peti­tor in our home, and a fear­ful dis­ap­point­ment”. That re­la­tion­ship runs through *Independence Day*. {013-S09}
## Specific, so uni­ver­sal
“Most of my writ­ing is emo­tion­ally au­to­bi­o­graph­i­cal,” Springsteen wrote. That, Varma said, is why it reaches any­one: true to him, and true to ev­ery­one else. {013-C07}

*Darkness on the Edge of Town* is “just beau­ti­ful, sim­ple lan­guage, and ev­ery­one re­lates”, he said. The method works even on a “non-metaphysical sub­ject” like lust: in *I’m on Fire* the singer wakes with “a sheet soak­ing wet and a freight train run­ning through the mid­dle of my head”. {013-R18}

~ Varma also read Springsteen on the six­ties: friends who were “real drug ex­per­i­ment­ing rad­i­cals”, and a con­struc­tion-worker brother-in-law who “re­mained his whole life a man of the fifties”.

quote.text: I’ve learned you’ve got to pull up the things that mean some­thing to you in order for them to mean any­thing to your au­di­ence.
quote.who: Bruce Springsteen, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: Aspect three: words
sections.head: Plain speech, deep water
sections.caption: simple words that go deeper
body: Shakespeare was the box-office su­per­star of his day, Amit Varma said, be­cause he wrote in the speak­ing rhythms of the day. Springsteen does the same: he never uses a word you can’t un­der­stand.

Simple is not shal­low. *Secret Garden* seems car­nal, then be­comes a song about how you can never truly know an­other per­son. *Brilliant Disguise* asks whether a lover is wear­ing a mask, and ends by turn­ing on the singer: “I damn sure don’t trust my­self.” {013-C08}
Ajay Shah’s ex­am­ple was *Racing in the Street*, which be­gins as a song about cars and half­way through be­comes “a psy­cho­log­i­cal dive into the mind of a deeply sad per­son”. {#racing}
## Endings mat­ter

Shah looks for a snap short sen­tence after a long one, “that power of four words, five words”. Varma pointed to Springsteen on chil­dren: “They are God giv­ing you an­other shot.” It ends on a mute sound, he said. {013-C09}
Springsteen had found his voice by his late 20s. “What shit were we doing in our late 20s?” Varma asked. Shah: “We were writ­ing re­ally bad shit.” {013-J06}
~ Even Springsteen fal­ters, Varma said. Of two sen­tences in a row in the mem­oir, the first “is crap”; the sec­ond “com­pletely nails it”.

quote.text: Great poets know how you end a line mat­ters.

sections.label: Aspect four: change
sections.head: Never his own tribute act
sections.caption: a career of constant change
body: Springsteen was de­ter­mined not to be one of those mu­si­cians “al­ways play­ing cover ver­sions of him­self”, Amit Varma said. As a boy, Varma heard a live *Growing Up* pre­ceded by what seemed like half an hour of talk, and was en­tranced. {#growingup}
“Songs shift their mean­ings when you sing them,” Springsteen once said. There are 30, 40, 50 ver­sions of *The River*, Varma said. {013-C10}

He nearly cut the piano from *Backstreets* be­fore Jon Landau talked him out of it. Greil Marcus later heard in that open­ing music “so stately, so heart­break­ing that it might be the pre­lude to a rock and roll ver­sion of the *Iliad*”. {#iliad}
## The right play­ers

For his band, Springsteen wanted nei­ther a one-man, one-vote democ­racy, “a tick­ing time bomb”, nor a name­less back­ing band. “You’re not look­ing for the best play­ers,” he wrote. “You’re look­ing for the right play­ers who click into some­thing unique.”

Ajay Shah car­ried the idea to com­pa­nies. Success cor­rodes equal part­ner­ships, he said, as Simon and Garfunkel found; teams need shared val­ues more than the world’s best drum­mer or tech­nol­o­gist. {013-C11}
~ Shah re­called Paul McCartney sup­pos­edly say­ing Ringo Starr “was not even the best drum­mer in the Beatles”. Varma thought Paul too self-effacing for that.

quote.text: Songs shift their mean­ings when you sing them. They shift their mean­ings in time. They shift their mean­ings with who you sing them with.
quote.who: Bruce Springsteen, as read by Amit Varma

quote.text: We each of us are adding to the lin­ear com­bi­na­tion of other people’s ex­pe­ri­ences. And I think that’s a great re­spon­si­bil­ity that we each of us should be the best ver­sion of our­selves be­cause we are in­flu­enc­ing so many peo­ple.

p3.title: Liner notes
p3.deck: Four stories behind the songs, and what each one teaches

stories.kicker: From the memoir: a boy, a rented guitar and an audience
stories.head: The show before the chords
body: Bruce Springsteen was seven when he de­cided he had to have a gui­tar. He had heard some­thing, or seen a pho­to­graph, and was struck. His mother could not af­ford to buy one, so she rented one.
For a few days the boy tried to play it. He sim­ply could not fig­ure it out.

Then came the sunny morn­ing when it had to go back. He took it out to the back­yard, where six or so of the neigh­bour­hood kids were gath­ered, and gave what he called “my first and last show for quite a while”. {013-S03}

Amit Varma read the memoir’s ac­count: “I held the gui­tar, I shook it, I shouted at it, I banged on it, I sang voodoo non­sense. I did ev­ery­thing but play it, all to their laugh­ter and great amuse­ment. I sucked.”
That af­ter­noon he re­turned the gui­tar, “sad but a lit­tle re­lieved”. Yet for a mo­ment in front of those kids, he wrote, he had smelled blood.

Later he got a gui­tar of his own, but did not know how to tune it. With the strings in what­ever state they were in, he wrote a few tunes and played in front of the mir­ror, sure he was re­ally cool.
Then some­one tuned it for him, and taught him how. He re­alised that ev­ery­thing he had done be­fore was rub­bish.
~ For Varma, that is “such a great metaphor for how step by step by step we learn so much about the craft”. {#untuned}
stories.why: Mastery be­gins with in­com­pe­tence plus de­sire. The boy could not play, but wanted it badly enough to put on a show any­way; the tuned gui­tar then showed him how much of the craft he had yet to learn.
stories.postscript: Max Weinberg, the E Street Band’s drum­mer, once said he had never seen any­one work as hard as Bruce Springsteen.

pic.caption: Amit Varma (right) on a rented guitar, with Ajay Shah

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on two demands for a hit, and the answers
stories.head: Want a hit? Have three
body: Bruce Springsteen turned in his debut, *Greetings from Asbury Park*, and Clive Davis handed it back: no hits, noth­ing for the radio. Springsteen went to the beach and wrote *Spirit in the Night*, then broke out his rhyming dic­tio­nary for *Blinded by the Light*.
Many artists, Amit Varma said, would in­sist on stay­ing true to their art. “Springsteen doesn’t do that. He says, Fuck it, you want a hit, I’ll write you a hit.” {013-S06}

It hap­pened again in 1984. *Born in the USA* was done when Jon Landau said they still needed a hit. {#landauhit} Furious, Springsteen went to his room and, as Varma imag­ined it, turned what he felt right then into *Dancing in the Dark*.
~ The tune is up­beat. The lyrics, Varma noted, are de­pres­sive: “I ain’t noth­ing but tired. Man, I’m just tired and bored with my­self.”
stories.why: Constraint can be raw ma­te­rial. Where many artists treat a com­mer­cial de­mand as an in­sult to their art, Springsteen took it as a chal­lenge, and his ir­ri­ta­tion be­came some of his best songs.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the hits written in a temper

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a song left on Elvis’s answering machine
stories.head: Elvis didn’t call back
body: One fine day Bruce Springsteen wrote a song called *Fire*, and heard in its lilt an Elvis Presley song. He got hold of Presley’s num­ber and called. The call went to an an­swer­ing ma­chine, so Springsteen sang the song into it and dic­tated the lyrics.
Presley ig­nored him. Springsteen gave the song to the Pointer Sisters, who made it a num­ber-one hit; his own later live ver­sions are, to Ajay Shah, the best.

Shah took a rule for life from it. “I learned one thing, which is just gift your stuff away,” he said. “Don’t try to hold ev­ery­thing, don’t try to hang on to ev­ery­thing.” {013-S10} All his life, he has given re­search ideas away freely.
~ Shah had paused mid-story for the young: “Oh, ye young reader, please go Google what is an an­swer­ing ma­chine.” {013-J07}

quote.text: It’s bet­ter to keep on in­vent­ing and giv­ing things away rather than try­ing to pro­tect one­self that, oh, this is my idea.

stories.postscript: Amit Varma’s foot­note: The Replacements once asked, “How do you say good­night to an an­swer­ing ma­chine?” {013-R26}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the song Elvis never returned

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a family drama that became a song
stories.head: Union card and wedding coat
body: Bruce Springsteen’s sis­ter Virginia be­came preg­nant at 17, dropped out of high school and mar­ried the fa­ther, Mickey Shave. In Springsteen’s telling, Mickey was an ar­ro­gant, leather-jacketed, bull-riding greaser from Lakewood, and even­tu­ally an all-round great guy.
Virginia, who “had never boiled water, washed a dish, or swept a floor”, be­came a hard­core Irish work­ing woman. Mickey worked in con­struc­tion.
“Which song did this in­spire?” Amit Varma asked. Ajay Shah got there first: “I got a job work­ing in con­struc­tion.”
It was *The River*, in which Mary is sev­en­teen and the nar­ra­tor, for his 19th birth­day, gets “a union card and a wed­ding coat”. {#mary}
~ Springsteen needed no myths. “His sis­ter gets preg­nant and gets mar­ried, he writes about that,” Varma said. {013-S08}
stories.why: Ordinary fam­ily drama was enough. When his writ­ing stu­dents ask what to write about, Varma tells them to look around them: Springsteen’s sis­ter, his fa­ther and his town were all the ma­te­rial he needed.

quiz.a: Jon Landau, who later be­came Springsteen’s pro­ducer and a fa­ther fig­ure to him.

quiz.a: Elvis Presley, via an an­swer­ing ma­chine; the Pointer Sisters took it to num­ber one.

quiz.a: About ten min­utes to write it, and thirty sec­onds to mix it.

quiz.a: A gov­ern­ment ploy to get peo­ple mar­ried so that they would pay more taxes.

quiz.a: It opens with a wall of sound and ends on the alaap.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 13. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Ludwig van Beethoven (Joseph Karl Stieler, public domain); Bruce Springsteen (Raph_PH, CC BY 4.0); Cormac McCarthy (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Jorge Luis Borges (Grete Stern, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Apple and Wikipedia.

shelf.creator: Philippe Margotin and Jean-Michel Guesdon
shelf.why: It tells the story be­hind every sin­gle Springsteen song, and Amit pairs it with the mem­oir as two won­der­ful books.

shelf.title: The Notebook Trilogy (The Notebook, The Proof, The Third Lie)
shelf.creator: Agota Kristof
shelf.why: Agota Kristof fled Hungary, learned French as an adult and wrote these nov­els in it, strip­ping prose and nar­ra­tive to the bone with enor­mous power.

shelf.title: Jhumpa Lahiri on Conversations with Tyler
shelf.creator: Tyler Cowen
shelf.why: A great in­ter­view in which Jhumpa Lahiri dis­cusses learn­ing Italian from scratch as an adult and writ­ing a book in it, and names Agota Kristof as a model.

shelf.title: Truth and Beauty
shelf.creator: S Chandrasekhar
shelf.why: A ‘lovely slim book’ that Ajay says ev­ery­body should read.

shelf.title: Independence Day
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: It’s about fa­thers and sons, and Ajay sees in it the drama of small towns all over India: de­spair, the dark­ness at the edge of town, fam­ily con­flict, the de­ci­sion to leave, and the lost so­cial net­work after you go.

shelf.title: Father and Son
shelf.creator: Cat Stevens
shelf.why: Ajay once found it a lit­tle clichéd, but twenty years on he thinks it’s a re­ally great song, so don’t worry that it’s too fa­mous.

shelf.title: The Road
shelf.creator: Cormac McCarthy
shelf.why: A fa­ther and son walk through a post-apocalyptic land­scape: Ajay says it takes you deep in­side what it means to be a fa­ther and a son, and it is his image of the bar­barism that would fol­low if civilisation’s ma­te­rial base dis­ap­peared.

shelf.title: Self-Portrait
shelf.creator: AK Ramanujan
shelf.why: A tiny poem on the same theme: the speaker re­sem­bles ‘ev­ery­one but myself’ and sees in shop win­dows the por­trait of a stranger, ‘often signed in a cor­ner by my father’.

shelf.title: Born to Run (acoustic live version)
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: The wall-of-sound album ver­sion didn’t suit his taste at the time.

shelf.title: The Promise (version on 18 Tracks)
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: Ajay sees Born to Run, Thunder Road and The Promise as a triad: ‘three win­dows into the same peo­ple, into the same life’.

shelf.title: Jungleland
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: Stairway to Heaven starts with an alaap and builds.

shelf.title: Racing in the Street
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: It starts as a young-man-and-cars song about il­le­gal street rac­ing.

shelf.title: Devils and Dust
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: Springsteen said it wrote it­self after a life­time of craft; Ajay calls it ‘one of those sweet and per­fect songs’.

shelf.title: Dancing in the Dark
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: A mas­ter­piece with lev­els: de­pres­sive lyrics (‘tired and bored with myself’) set to an up­beat tune.

shelf.title: The River
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great song whose open­ing sec­tion is bril­liant.

shelf.title: Darkness on the Edge of Town
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: ‘Just beau­ti­ful, sim­ple lan­guage, and ev­ery­one re­lates.’ It is spe­cific to his life, yet any­one any­where can see them­selves in it.

shelf.title: I’m on Fire
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: The ap­proach works even on a ‘non-metaphysical’ sub­ject like lust.

shelf.title: Secret Garden
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: It seems car­nal at first, then turns into a song about how you can never truly know an­other per­son and the re­cesses in each of us no one else can reach.

shelf.title: Brilliant Disguise
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: It be­gins by ask­ing whether the lover is wear­ing a mask and ends by turn­ing the gaze on him­self (‘I damn sure don’t trust myself’).

shelf.title: Backstreets
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: Greil Marcus wrote that it ‘be­gins with music so stately, so heart­break­ing that it might be the pre­lude to a rock and roll ver­sion of the Iliad’.

shelf.title: Atlantic City (from Nebraska)
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: Amit calls it a mas­ter­piece and Nebraska ‘such a great stripped down album’.

shelf.title: Growing Up (live)
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: Before the song, Springsteen talked for what seemed like half an hour, and it was bril­liant.

shelf.title: You’re Missing
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: The Springsteen song that gave the show its name and world­view: its line ‘ev­ery­thing is everything’ points at all the world’s won­ders while mark­ing someone’s ab­sence.

shelf.title: TB Sheets
shelf.creator: Van Morrison
shelf.why: Another great long song, by Van Morrison, a hero to both Springsteen and Amit.

shelf.title: Answering Machine
shelf.creator: The Replacements
shelf.why: A great song with an im­mor­tal line, ‘How do you say good­night to an an­swer­ing ma­chine?’, whose sad­ness is lost on peo­ple who never used one.

shelf.title: Pearl Jam’s live and bootleg albums
shelf.creator: Pearl Jam
shelf.why: In the late ‘90s and early 2000s they gave Amit the same joy as Springsteen’s live record­ings: ‘all of their live al­bums are just so incredible’.

shelf.title: Like a Rolling Stone: Bob Dylan at the Crossroads
shelf.creator: Greil Marcus
shelf.why: Amit calls Marcus a ge­nius music writer whose phrases cap­ture what lis­ten­ers feel but can’t ar­tic­u­late.

shelf.title: Critic Declares Springsteen Future of Rock and Roll
shelf.creator: Mass Moments
shelf.why: The back­ground to the night that started the Landau-Springsteen part­ner­ship.

shelf.title: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
shelf.creator: Ludwig Wittgenstein
shelf.why: Wittgenstein’s great book, whose line ‘whereof one can­not speak, thereof one must be silent’ Amit loves and uses to argue that any one lan­guage is in­ad­e­quate.

shelf.title: On Exactitude in Science
shelf.creator: Jorge Luis Borges
shelf.why: Borges’s one-paragraph para­ble of car­tog­ra­phers whose per­fectly ac­cu­rate map is as large as the em­pire and out of date the next mo­ment: no rep­re­sen­ta­tion can fully cap­ture re­al­ity.

shelf.title: How This Nobel Has Redefined Literature
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It ar­gues that the Nobel hon­oured the prize more than the man, and that lit­er­a­ture is words and sto­ry­telling, not just books.

shelf.title: Dhano Dhanne
shelf.creator: Jaya Varma and the Chandigarh Choir
shelf.why: A per­sonal bonus, ‘be­cause hey, why not?’

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

laughs.text: Amit on the two kinds of BS in Ajay’s life: Business Standard, where he’s been a colum­nist ‘for the last sixty-three years or some­thing like that’, and Bruce Springsteen.
Ajay: ‘You’re at episode thir­teen of Everything is Everything… who knows where we’ll be.’ Amit: ‘Are you com­par­ing us to Springsteen? Don’t you dare do that.’
Ajay, mid-Elvis story: ‘Oh ye young reader, please go Google what is an an­swer­ing ma­chine.’

Ajay re­calls Paul McCartney sup­pos­edly say­ing Ringo ‘was not even the best drum­mer in the Beatles’ (Amit finds Paul too self-effacing for that). Amit then di­gresses into cricket: Mark Waugh said some­thing sim­i­lar about Steve, and Mark’s nick­name is ‘Afghanistan’, be­cause he’s the for­got­ten Waugh.

Wittgenstein (‘whereof one can­not speak, thereof one must be silent’) and Borges’s map as big as the world, which is out of date the mo­ment it’s drawn. Amit riffs on the old river say­ing: ‘You do not step in the same map twice.’ Later Ajay of­fers his own twist: ‘no man can sing the same song twice.’

McCarthy’s post-apocalyptic walk of father and son
Song Ajay hears in every live version, in order
Ajay’s word for the show; never Springsteen’s
Borges’s, as big as the world
Chess and poker jargon for producing a lot
Song of a union card and a wedding coat
Band outplayed at a San Francisco audition
Song written in ten minutes, mixed in thirty seconds
Rented instrument a seven-year-old could not play
Song sung into an answering machine
Bonnie, headliner on Landau’s famous night
Slow opening that Jungleland saves for the end
Agota, who learned French at twenty-one
Love songs were a ploy to raise these, thought Springsteen’s father
